title: Number of Matching Subsequences
hints: checking each word against s independently rescans s over and over - what if many words could advance through s together in a single pass?
think of each word as a pointer sitting at some position in itself, waiting for its next required character to show up in s
group all these waiting pointers into buckets keyed by 'the character they're currently waiting for'

scan s once, character by character; at each character c, take every pointer waiting for c, advance it by one position, and re-bucket it under its new next-required character (or mark it complete if it just consumed its word's last character)

a trie isn't strictly required here, but it helps you avoid re-deriving each word's next character from scratch by walking shared prefixes together - insert words into a trie and let 'waiting pointers' be trie node references instead of raw string indices
commonMistakes: resetting a word's progress instead of resuming from where it left off when its character appears again later in s
not counting duplicate words in the list separately
off-by-one when checking whether a word's pointer has fully consumed the word (completion check)

content.problemStatement:
You're given a space-delimited string of lowercase `words` and a separate base string `s`.

**Count how many entries in the word list are a subsequence of `s`, meaning their characters appear in the same relative order in `s`, not necessarily contiguous.**

Count each entry separately, so a word appearing twice in the list that matches counts twice.
constraints: s and every word consist only of lowercase English letters
notes: a word longer than s (can never be a subsequence)
the same word repeated multiple times in the list
a word that uses every character of s in order (an exact match)

sampleTestCases.explanation: "a" is a subsequence (trivially); "bb" is not (s only has one b); "acd" and "ace" both are

optimal.time: O(total word characters + len(s) * 26) roughly, a big improvement over rescanning s per word when there are many words
optimal.pattern: insert all words into a trie annotated with which words end at each node; scan s once, and at each character, advance every 'active' trie pointer that has a matching child (bucket pointers by the next character they're waiting for, similar to the classic multi-pointer/queue solution but framed via trie structure)

bruteForce.approach: for each word, use a two-pointer scan over s to check if the word is a subsequence
bruteForce.time: O(n * len(s)) where n is the number of words
bruteForce.space: O(1) beyond the split word list
